text:
Sheet 02 · 500 to 1,200 ft


  
    
      
    
    Scale 1:1
    Duc (Bill) Le
  

  
    Hi, I'm Bill
    My name is Duc Le, and most people call me Bill. I'm in my last year of an MS in Supply Chain Management at the University of Houston's Bauer College of Business, and I work in procurement at Oliden Technology in Stafford, which builds MWD/LWD and rotary steerable tools.
    Most of my work is the part nobody sees: finding shops that can machine a part to print, keeping orders in step with drawing changes, and checking that what arrives is what we asked for. I like that the job sits between engineering, finance, and the supplier, and that a late part means a late tool.
    At school I'm learning to back that work with data. This site collects what I've built, mostly in R.

title: Rig count forecast
text:
Project overview

Two or three sentences: the business question, what the analysis found, and what someone should do about it. Written last.

title: Rig count forecast
text:
Problem statement
A company that builds downhole tools has to order some parts long before it needs them. Machined housings and specialty alloys can take months to arrive. How many tools customers want depends on how much drilling is going on, so a buyer planning those orders wants to know: how many rigs will be running six months from now, and how sure can we be?

title: Rig count forecast
text:
Approach

Planned steps:

Pull the weekly US rig count and roll it up to monthly
Plot the trend and look for seasonal patterns with ggplot2
Fit and compare ETS and ARIMA models with the fable package
Test accuracy on a held-back year of data
Turn the forecast range into an ordering rule for long-lead parts

The R code, with comments, goes here. Each step becomes a short section with its code chunk and one line on why.

title: Rig count forecast
text:
Results and impact

The forecast chart with its range, and what it means for when to place long-lead orders. Charts made with ggplot2 (with hover, using ggiraph), each with a line on what it means for the business.

title: Late delivery risk

Two or three sentences: the business question, what the analysis found, and what someone should do about it. Written last.

title: Late delivery risk
text:
Problem statement
On-time delivery is one of the first things a buyer checks on a supplier. If you could tell which orders are likely to ship late before they do, you could expedite the right ones and stop chasing the rest. The question: which orders are likely to ship late, and what drives it?

title: Late delivery risk
text:
Approach

Planned steps:

Load the order data and clean dates, types, and missing values
Compare late rates by shipping mode, region, and product category
Fit a logistic regression and a decision tree
Compare the two with a confusion matrix and ROC curve
Turn the strongest drivers into plain rules a buyer can use

The R code, with comments, goes here. Each step becomes a short section with its code chunk and one line on why.

title: Oilfield services health check
text:
Problem statement
SLB, Halliburton, and Baker Hughes are three of the largest oilfield services companies, and big buyers of downhole tools and parts. When oil prices fall, drilling slows, and so do their orders. For a supplier, or someone hoping to work for one, the question is: how closely does each company move with oil prices, and which looks steadiest?

title: Oilfield services health check
text:
Approach

Planned steps:

Pull daily stock prices and WTI crude prices with tidyquant
Compute returns and rolling correlations with oil
Compare revenue and margins from annual reports
Chart how each company held up through the 2020 oil price crash and since

title: Drill log
text:
Sheet 08 · Below TD
You made it past total depth. This page is for people who like to see how things are built.

How this site is built




Made with
R and Quarto in RStudio, hosted on GitHub Pages. The case studies are R Markdown files rendered straight into the site.


The idea
The site is drawn like an engineering drawing of a well. You don't scroll down a page so much as drill down through it.


Depth gauge
The ruler on the left counts feet as you scroll. Each page covers its own depth range.


Title block
The box in the corner, like the one on every engineering drawing: name, sheet, depth, revision. Press it to shrink it.


Lithology column
The striped strip next to the well on the home page. On a real mud log it shows the rock type at each depth: dots for sandstone, lines for shale, bricks for limestone.


Mud pulse
The orange dash that travels down the well. MWD tools send data to the surface as pressure pulses in the drilling mud. The row of dots at the top of each new page is the same idea.


Color rule
Ink on drafting paper, and in dark mode, white lines on blueprint blue. Safety orange marks only things you can press.


Type
Space Grotesk for headings, Be Vietnam Pro for body text (made by Vietnamese designers, so every accent mark sits right), Space Mono for labels.


Live well view
On the home page, the cross-section on the right drills as you scroll. The orange dots running up the pipe are mud pulses, and the specks are cuttings. The well kicks off at 3,000 ft and builds angle toward the target, like a real directional well.


ROP
Rate of penetration, shown in the title block and the live view. Here it's how fast you scroll, in feet per second. A real rig in hard rock might make 50 to 100 feet in an hour, so you're doing fine.


Sheet log
The title block counts the pages you've seen. Log all of them and this page opens on its own.


Toolkit
Drawn as a bottom-hole assembly: the string of tools right above the bit. Skills without proof yet are listed as parts on order.


Record player
The turntable in the corner runs the music. Press it to play or pause, and press the dots to flip the record. The A-side is made live in your browser with the Web Audio API: warm electric piano, soft bass, a lazy beat, and two slower tracks with strings and a plucked lead. Nothing is recorded, so there's nothing to license. The B-side is Bill's own favorites, played by YouTube's player.


Journey map
The route on the home page draws itself when you reach it. Press a stop to light up that part of the timeline.


Career log
On the resume, the same history is drawn as a strip log, the way a well log shows what's at each depth. Press a bar to jump to the entry.


Headshot
Printed in ink in light mode and as a cyanotype in dark mode, which is how real blueprints were made. Hover to see it in color.
